name: Does a high variance premium lead prices

sections.hypothesis: Weeks that start while implied volatility sits unusually far above realised volatility (a high variance risk premium) are followed by better BTC (ETH) returns than other weeks.
sections.rationale: Who pays: option buyers pay for protection. When implied volatility (what insurance costs) runs well above realised (what moves have been), holders of risk are being paid more to bear it, and in equities that premium forecasts the market's returns over the next months: Bollerslev, Tauchen and Zhou (2009, Review of Financial Studies, 'Expected stock returns and variance risk premia'). Crypto evidence is thin (checked 2026-11-22): no paper found that tests whether Bitcoin's premium predicts returns; 'Risk premia in the Bitcoin market' (arXiv 2410.15195, 2024, Deribit options) measures it and finds it highest in the calm regime, and Alexander and Imeraj's Bitcoin VIX work (Journal of Alternative Investments) covers only 2019-20. So this study is the test, not a replication. Danger, stated now: the premium peaks after crashes, so this could be Fear & Greed contrarian or dip-buying, both rejected, in disguise; the control below is built for exactly that. Disclosed as near a rejected family. History is short: DVOL starts 2021-03.
sections.rules: kestrel signal-study variance-premium BTCUSDT ETHUSDT. Daily premium = Deribit's DVOL close (30-day implied volatility, annualised %, BTC and ETH) minus realised volatility over the last 30 days from Binance daily log returns (annualised %, the same 365-day convention), both known at the 00:00 UTC close. The signal is on when the mean premium over the 7 days to the Sunday close is above its median over the 180 days before those 7. Span: from the first Sunday with 187 days of DVOL to 2025-10. Each Sunday's daily close (UTC) is a sample; outcome: the log return of the Binance coin to the next Sunday's close. Samples a week apart never overlap; BTC and ETH are pooled (they move together, so the effective sample is smaller than the count). Never the holdout. Run once.
sections.falsification: PROCEED only if P(spread > 0) is at least 90% (bootstrap), the spread (mean week after 'on' minus mean week after 'off') beats one round trip of costs (about 22 bps), and the independence control holds. Otherwise KILL. A PROCEED leads to a strategy note on the full scorecard (BTC and ETH's holdout years are spent, so it would be judged forward on paper); a KILL ends it. Its overlap with the pursued strategies is reported beside the result, deciding nothing. The independence control, fixed here: the spread is also measured separately in weeks whose past week rose and weeks whose past week fell. PROCEED needs the spread positive in both halves as well; if it lives in only one, the signal is momentum (or dip-buying, a rejected family) under another name, and that is a KILL, said plainly.
sections.parameters: None to choose: 30 days (DVOL's own horizon), 7 days, the 180-day median fixed here.
sections.costs: A study: one look. Data: Deribit's public volatility-index endpoint (free, no key). DVOL is Deribit's own index of its options; its method could change and that is a caveat.

history.reason: Rejected (Luke, 2026-11-22). KILL (findings 22): spread +0.73%, P 81%; +1.45% after falls, -0.20% after rises: the control fails, dip-buying in disguise.
